newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London recoverd from an earlier bout of origin selling as arbitrage and speculative buyers moved into nearby positions. All positions ended firmer but off highs. November added $13.00 to close at $1,527. In New York, arabica futures continued their upward move led by steep gains in the spot December contract.

Supplies are expected to remain tight within the next few weeks and prices should remain firm. Traders said it would probably be another four to six weeks until coffee coming in from Central America would build stockpiles.

Supply woes re-emerged at the end of September when the CSCE reported exchange-certified stocks fell to their lowest level in 12 years. After the close the CSCE reported another small fall in certified stocks which could aid sentiment.

Traders said it now seems with delays in the crops, problems getting supplies out of Colombia and overcommitments by others, there is a scramble for October/November coffees. However, once new crop supplies start to become availabe, prices are expected to come down.

UNITED STATES - Certified coffee stocks for delivery at the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange showed another small decline by 945 bags to 30,724 (31,669) bags after the fall by 10,433 bags the previous week. Stocks in New York, New Orleans and San Francisco remained unchanged at 4,811, 18,644 and 6,000 bags, respectively. However, stocks in Miami fell by 945 bags to 1,269 bags (2,214 bags).

COLOMBIA - According to the National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF), the 1995/96 coffee year was the worst since the collapse of the International Coffee Agreement in 1989. It was added that coffee will face problems also in 1996/97.

ANIF predicted that the National Coffee Fund, which uses the proceeds of coffee sales to purchase the new crop from growers, will post a 120 billion peso-deficit for the 1995/96 coffee year three times higher than forecast.

It was added that if the peso's strengthening and inflation continue unchecked, production costs will rise at the same time as export profits fall leading to a deficit of more than 180 billion pesos in 1996/97.

MALAYSIA - Malaysia imported 183,300 bags of coffee in October/April 1995/96, which compares to 155,800 bags the same period in 1994/95. Total imports in crop year 1994/95 (October/September) reached 278,300 bags.

The main suppliers of green coffee in October/April 1995/96 were Indonesia (100,600 vs 72,200 bags) and Vietnam (24,300 vs 18,700 bags). The country exported 76,100 bags of coffee in October/April 1995/96, which compares to 33,000 bags the same period in 1994/95. Total exports in crop year 1994/95 reached 77,500 bags.

TAIWAN - Taiwan imported 13,300 bags of coffee in June 1996, down from 15,000 bags imported the previous month. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 46,600 bags. Exports in June 1996 were 5,700 bags with total exports in January/March 1996 at 24,000 bags.
